editor_spans.body: Over five days the government's Ukraine statements followed one thread, and it was energy. When Mr Burnham reported to the Commons on 12 October, he did not present the energy ceasefire mainly as a humanitarian step. He presented it as a way to get diesel back onto world markets 'without rewarding the aggressor'. With the Middle East conflict also squeezing supply, the government has two goals that pull against each other. It wants Russian energy revenue cut off: sanctions now cover more than 90% of Russia's oil-producing capacity, and it is pushing partners to copy its ban on shipping and insuring Russian LNG. It also wants energy prices down at home. A ceasefire between the two sides was the only way to pursue both goals at once.

That is why it matters that Russia struck energy infrastructure after President Trump called for the ceasefire. The government's response to the US–Russia agreement was unusually defensive in tone. It spoke of energy markets and the cost of living, and repeated that it 'fully supports US-led efforts'. That reads like a government whose interests depend on a deal it did not negotiate. If the ceasefire fails, the cost-of-living pressure returns, and London has little leverage of its own to stop that.

Read the 'doubling down' headline against the numbers. The missile announcement is £45 million, and only £10 million of it is being brought forward for winter. It sits on top of £1.6 billion for LMMs that was already committed over four years. The new elements are timing and a request to ministers to draw up packages. Nothing has yet been decided on scale. Watch whether the 'coming weeks' bring new money or only repackage commitments already made.

The most important line of the week was buried in a statement about the UN. The Prime Minister said the UK should open 'a serious dialogue about the different options' for its long-term relationship with the EU. He called keeping the status quo a 'dereliction of duty' and promised that 'the British public will be the boss'. That last phrase suggests public consent, perhaps a public vote, at some later stage. Before saying so, he set out ten years of practical costs: salmon checks, banned seed potatoes and shellfish, and £200 export certificates. This builds the case for a bigger change than a better summit deal in Brussels on 20 November.

Mr Burnham is running national government the way he ran Greater Manchester as mayor. That means things put 'back in public hands', a No10 North, and power pushed down to regions. The offer to Holyrood is also political. By calling the Scottish Government one of Europe's most centralised devolved administrations, it turns the language of devolution against the party that has long claimed it.

The Derby announcement deserves a closer look. The HQ will hold up to 450 staff and will not be finished until spring 2029, close to the next general election. The skilled rail jobs that really anchor Derby are at Alstom's train works. Credit for the fares freeze goes to public ownership, but a freeze is a political choice, not a result of ownership itself. The long-term problem is that fewer than 7% of rail workers are under 25. Against that ageing workforce, 600 apprentices over four years is a modest start, not a solution.
